newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia bids farewell to late President Barco.
newsitem.headline: Colombia bids farewell to late President Barco.

text.p: Colombia offered a solemn farewell on Thursday to Virgilio Barco Vargas, the former president who led his country through one of the most difficult and violent periods in the nation's modern history.
Barco, who held office from 1986 to 1990, died on Tuesday after a long battle with stomach cancer and Alzheimer's disease. He was 75.

In a speech at the National Cathedral, overlooking Bogota's historic Plaza de Bolivar square, President Ernesto Samper paid homage to the man whose administration declared open war on narcotics trafficking and saw drug-related violence soar to bloody heights.
"Barco taught us to fight against organised crime, to resist the onslaught of terrorism and to say no to violence," Samper said.
He noted that Barco had also stressed the dual nature of the drug war, however, by campaigning tirelessly for the need to fight against "the vice of millions of consumers worldwide."

Hundreds of people, including three presidential candidates, an attorney general and scores of police, judges and judicial officials, were killed in the late 1980s as drug lords waged a campaign of assassinations and bombings against their threatened extradition to the United States.

Barco, a soft-spoken but tough politician, was the only Colombian leader to date to have ordered the extradition of a top drug lord. He responded stoically to the wave of violence by forging close ties with Washington and declaring an all-out war against the infamous Medellin cartel.
It was one of the cartel's masterminds, Carlos Lehder, who Barco bundled off to the United States aboard a U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration aircraft in 1987.

Unlike the leaders of the powerful Cali drug mob, recently sentenced by a Colombian judge to terms that could see them walk free in as little as five years, Lehder's U.S. judge gave him life without parole, plus 135 years.

A constitutional ban was clamped on extradition a year after Barco left office. But his state funeral, held on a typically gray and rainy afternoon in this Andean city, came on the same day that the Senate was to vote on a bill that would revive the controversial practice.

Former Venezuelan president Carlos Andres Perez, two former Colombian presidents, the entire diplomatic corps in Bogota and a host of top government and military officials were among those on hand for Barco's funeral. It capped three days of national mourning during which his body lay in state in the Capitol.

Friends, family and well-wishers waving white handkerchiefs shouted "Long Live Barco" and tossed flowers at the former president's coffin. It was mounted atop a gun carriage and draped in the yellow, blue and red national flag as it passed slowly through the downtown area en route to Bogota's Central Cemetery.
Barco, who is survived by his wife, Carolina Isakson de Barco and four children, was later buried in a plot set aside for former heads of state.
